nodes.statement_short: Bound the annulus error term by three pieces.

nodes.name: pointwise bound on the annulus
nodes.statement:
To prove \eqref{est0}, we use the above properties of $u_k$ and $w_k$ to observe that  egin{multline} \left|\int_{R<|x|<R+a}\Big[|
abla v_{n_k}|^2-|
abla u_k|^2-|
abla w_k|^2 - rac{c}{|x|^2}\left(|v_{n_k}|^2-|u_k|^2-|w_k|^2ight)\Big]dxight| \ \leqslant 5\int_{R<|x|<R+a}|
abla v_{n_k}|^2dx+4a^{-2}\int_{R<|x|<R+a}|v_{n_k}|^2dx + rac{3c}{R^2}\int_{R<|x|<R+a}|v_{n_k}|^2dx. \end{multline}
nodes.statement_short: Bound the annulus integrand.

nodes.name: third term
nodes.statement: First, by choosing $R>0$ sufficiently large, we will have \begin{equation} \frac{3c}{R^2}\int_{R<|x|<R+a}|v_{n_k}|^2dx \leqslant \frac{3c}{R^2} \|v_{n_k}\|_{L^2}^2 \leqslant \frac{(c_*-c)\delta}{4} \quad\text{for all} \ k\in\mathbb{N}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Third term small for large $R$.

nodes.name: second term
nodes.statement: The second term in the right-hand side of \eqref{est} is handled using Step 1 with $|y_k|\to\infty$: for any fixed $R,a>0$, we have that \begin{equation} \lim_{k\to\infty} \int_{R<|x|<R+a}|v_{n_k}|^2dx=0. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Second term vanishes by Step 1.

nodes.name: first term
nodes.statement:
As for the first term, we claim that we can choose $R>0$ as large as we want and $a>0$ such that, up to a subsequence,  egin{equation} 5\int_{R<|x|<R+a}|
abla v_{n_k}|^2dx\leqslant  rac{(c_*-c)\delta}{4} \quad	ext{for all} \ k\in\mathbb{N}. \end{equation} Estimates \eqref{term3}--\eqref{term1} prove \eqref{est0}, and hence \eqref{e1}. If the above claim is not true, then using a diagonal argument we can construct a subsequence $\{v_{n_{k_l}}\}$, and a sequence of pairwise disjoint annuli \[ A_j=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^N : R_j<|x|<R_j+a_j\} \quad	ext{with}\quad R_{j+1}>R_j+a_j, \] such that, for all $j\in\{1,\dots,l\}$, \[ \int_{A_j}|
abla v_{n_{k_l}}|^2dx\geqslant  ar \delta:=  rac{(c_*-c)\delta}{20}>0 \quad	ext{for all} \ n_{k_l}\in\mathbb{N}. \] But then \[ \int_{\mathbb{R}^N}|
abla v_{n_{k_l}}|^2dx \geqslant \sum_{j\in\mathbb{N}}\int_{A_j}|
abla v_{n_{k_l}}|^2dx \geqslant \sum_{j=1}^l\int_{A_j}|
abla v_{n_{k_l}}|^2dx \geqslant l ar\delta, \] and it follows that \[ \lim_{l	o\infty}\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}|
abla v_{n_{k_l}}|^2dx=+\infty. \] In view of \eqref{hardy2} this contradicts \eqref{a}, and completes the proof of \eqref{e1}.
nodes.statement_short: First term small by a diagonal argument on disjoint annuli and boundedness of $H$.

nodes.name: contradiction via Gagliardo-Nirenberg
nodes.statement: We will now combine \eqref{e1} with the Gagliardo--Nirenberg inequality \eqref{GN} and the assumption on the energy in \eqref{a} to reach a contradiction. Using Step 1 with $|y_k|\to\infty$, we have that $u_k\to0$ in $L^{p+1}(\mathbb{R}^N)$. Hence, by \eqref{a}, \begin{align*} \limsup_{k\rightarrow\infty}H(v_{n_k})\leqslant\frac{2}{p+1}\liminf_{k\rightarrow\infty}\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}|v_{n_k}|^{p+1}dx =\frac{2}{p+1}\liminf_{k\rightarrow\infty}\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}|w_k|^{p+1}dx, \end{align*} and so, by \eqref{e1}, \begin{align} \liminf_{k\rightarrow\infty}H(w_k)<\frac{2}{p+1}\liminf_{k\rightarrow\infty}\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}|w_k|^{p+1}dx. \end{align} Using again Step 1 with $|y_k|\to\infty$, we also have that $u_k\to0$ in $L^2(\mathbb{R}^N)$, which implies \[ M_\mathrm{gs}=\lim_{k\rightarrow\infty}\|v_{n_k}\|_{L^2} =\lim_{k\rightarrow\infty}\|w_k\|_{L^2}. \] Therefore, \eqref{GN} applied to $w_k$ yields \[ \frac{2}{p+1}\liminf_{k\rightarrow\infty}\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}|w_k|^{p+1}dx \leqslant\liminf_{k\rightarrow\infty}\left(\frac{\|w_k\|_{L^2}}{M_\mathrm{gs}}\right)^{\frac4N}H(w_k) = \liminf_{k\rightarrow\infty}H(w_k), \] which, together with \eqref{e4}, leads to the contradiction \[ \liminf_{k\rightarrow\infty}H(w_k)<\liminf_{k\rightarrow\infty}H(w_k). \] This shows that $\lim_{k\to\infty}\mathrm{I}_k=0$ and completes the proof of \eqref{zerolimit}.
nodes.statement_short: GN inequality applied to $w_k$ contradicts (4.13).

nodes.name: positive limiting energy
nodes.statement:
We now have  egin{align*} \liminf_{k	o\infty} E(v_{n_k}) &=\liminf_{k	o\infty}  rac12 \|
abla v_{n_k}\|_{L^2}^2 -\lim_{k	o\infty}  rac{1}{p+1} \| v_{n_k}\|_{L^{p+1}}^{p+1}\ &=\liminf_{k	o\infty}  rac12 \|
abla \widetilde{v}_{n_k}\|_{L^2}^2 -\lim_{k	o\infty}  rac{1}{p+1} \| \widetilde{v}_{n_k}\|_{L^{p+1}}^{p+1}\ &\geqslant  rac12 \|
abla v\|_{L^2}^2 -  rac{1}{p+1} \|v\|_{L^{p+1}}^{p+1}>E(v)\geqslant 0, \end{align*} where the last inequality follows from \eqref{posE} with $\|v\|_{L^2}=M_\mathrm{gs}$. This contradicts \eqref{a} and shows that the sequence $\{y_k\}$ must indeed be bounded in $\mathbb{R}^N$.
nodes.statement_short: Vanishing Hardy term gives $\liminf E(v_{n_k})>0$, contradiction.

nodes.name: Step 3: conclusion
nodes.statement: {\em Step~3: Conclusion.} Suppose, without loss of generality, that $y_k\to y^*\in\mathbb{R}^N$. Then \[ v_{n_k}\to v^*=v(\cdot+y^*) \quad \text{in} \quad L^q(\mathbb{R}^N), \quad \forall q\in[2,2^*), \] and $v_{n_k}\rightharpoonup v^*$ weakly in $H^1(\mathbb{R}^N)$. Since the Hardy functional $H$ is weakly lower semi-continuous \cite{montefusco}, and $p+1\in(2,2^*)$, it now follows by \eqref{posE} that \[ \begin{split} 0\leqslant E(v^*)=\frac{1}{2}H(v^*)-\frac{1}{p+1}\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}|v^*|^{p+1}dx &\leqslant \frac{1}{2}\limsup_{k\rightarrow\infty}H(v_{n_k})-\frac{1}{p+1}\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}|v^*|^{p+1}dx\\ &\phantom{\leqslant}=\limsup_{k\rightarrow\infty}E(v_{n_k})\leqslant 0, \end{split} \] so in fact \begin{equation} E(v^*)=0 \quad\text{and}\quad H(v^*)=\lim_{k\rightarrow\infty}H(v_{n_k}). \end{equation} Since $\|v^*\|_{L^2}=M_\mathrm{gs}$ and $E(v^*)=0$, Proposition \ref{charact.prop} yields $v^*=e^{i\gamma_0}Q_{\lambda_0}$ for some $\gamma_0\in\mathbb{R}$, $\lambda_0>0$, and some $Q\in \mathcal{G}$. Finally, by \eqref{convergence} and \eqref{hardy2}, we also have that $\|v_{n_k}\|_{H^1}\rightarrow \|v^*\|_{H^1}$. Hence $\{v_{n_k}\}$ converges strongly to $v^*$ in $H^1(\mathbb{R}^N)$, which completes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Limit has zero energy, is a ground state by Proposition 3, convergence upgrades to $H^1$.

nodes.name: convergence of the sequence
nodes.statement: {\em Step~3: Conclusion.} Suppose, without loss of generality, that $y_k\to y^*\in\mathbb{R}^N$. Then \[ v_{n_k}\to v^*=v(\cdot+y^*) \quad \text{in} \quad L^q(\mathbb{R}^N), \quad \forall q\in[2,2^*), \] and $v_{n_k}\rightharpoonup v^*$ weakly in $H^1(\mathbb{R}^N)$.
nodes.statement_short: Translations converge, so $v_{n_k}\to v^*$.

nodes.name: zero energy of the limit
nodes.statement: Since the Hardy functional $H$ is weakly lower semi-continuous \cite{montefusco}, and $p+1\in(2,2^*)$, it now follows by \eqref{posE} that \[ \begin{split} 0\leqslant E(v^*)=\frac{1}{2}H(v^*)-\frac{1}{p+1}\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}|v^*|^{p+1}dx &\leqslant \frac{1}{2}\limsup_{k\rightarrow\infty}H(v_{n_k})-\frac{1}{p+1}\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}|v^*|^{p+1}dx\\ &\phantom{\leqslant}=\limsup_{k\rightarrow\infty}E(v_{n_k})\leqslant 0, \end{split} \] so in fact \begin{equation} E(v^*)=0 \quad\text{and}\quad H(v^*)=\lim_{k\rightarrow\infty}H(v_{n_k}). \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Lower semicontinuity and (1.8) give $E(v^*)=0$ and $H$ convergence.

nodes.name: limit is a ground state
nodes.statement: Since $\|v^*\|_{L^2}=M_\mathrm{gs}$ and $E(v^*)=0$, Proposition \ref{charact.prop} yields $v^*=e^{i\gamma_0}Q_{\lambda_0}$ for some $\gamma_0\in\mathbb{R}$, $\lambda_0>0$, and some $Q\in \mathcal{G}$.
nodes.statement_short: Proposition 3 identifies $v^*$.

nodes.name: strong convergence
nodes.statement: Finally, by \eqref{convergence} and \eqref{hardy2}, we also have that $\|v_{n_k}\|_{H^1}\rightarrow \|v^*\|_{H^1}$. Hence $\{v_{n_k}\}$ converges strongly to $v^*$ in $H^1(\mathbb{R}^N)$, which completes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Norm convergence gives strong $H^1$ convergence.

nodes.name: regularization
nodes.statement: By regularization we may assume that $u$ is smooth enough for the following calculation.
nodes.statement_short: Assume $u$ smooth.

nodes.name: first derivative
nodes.statement:
Since $u$ satisfies (ef{inls}), we find \[  egin{split} \Gamma'(t)&=2\mathrm{Re}\int|x|^2 ar{u}\partial_tu=2\mathrm{Re}\int|x|^2 ar{u}i(\Delta u+ rac{c}{|x|^2}u+|u|^{p-1}u)\ &=-2\mathrm{Im}\int|x|^2( ar{u}\Delta u+ rac{c}{|x|^2}|u|^2+|u|^{p+1})=-2\mathrm{Im}\int|x|^2 ar{u}\Delta u. \end{split} \] Integrating by parts and using that $
abla |x|^2=2x$, we obtain \[ \Gamma'(t)=2\mathrm{Im}\int
abla u( ar{u}
abla|x|^2+|x|^2
abla ar{u})=4\mathrm{Im}\int ar{u}(
abla u\cdot x). \]
nodes.statement_short: Compute $\Gamma'$ by the equation and integration by parts.

nodes.name: second derivative
nodes.statement:
Using again integration by parts, we get \[  egin{split} \Gamma''(t)&=4\mathrm{Im}\int\partial_t ar{u}(x\cdot
abla u)+ ar{u}(x\cdot
abla\partial_tu) =4\mathrm{Im}\int\partial_tu[-x\cdot
abla ar{u}-
abla\cdot( ar{u}x)]\ &=4\mathrm{Im}\int\partial_tu[-2x\cdot
abla ar{u}- ar{u}
abla\cdot x] =-8\mathrm{Im}\int\partial_tu(x\cdot
abla ar{u})-4N\mathrm{Im}\int\partial_tu ar{u}. \end{split} \]
nodes.statement_short: Express $\Gamma''$ through two terms.

nodes.name: first term
nodes.statement: We use (\ref{inls}) to compute the last two terms. We first find \begin{align} -4N\mathrm{Im}\int\partial_tu\bar{u}&=-4N\mathrm{Re}\int\bar{u}(\Delta u+\frac{c}{|x|^2}u+|u|^{p-1}u)\notag \\ &=4N\int{|\nabla u|^2}-4Nc\int\frac{|u|^2}{|x|^2}-4N\int|u|^{p+1}. \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Compute $-4N\mathrm{Im}\int\partial_t u\bar u$.

nodes.name: second term split
nodes.statement:
Similarly, \[  egin{split} -8\mathrm{Im}\int\partial_tu(x\cdot 
abla  ar{u})&= -8\mathrm{Re}\int(x\cdot
abla ar{u})(\Delta u+ rac{c}{|x|^2}u+|u|^{p-1}u) \ &=-8\mathrm{Re}\int\Delta u(x\cdot
abla ar{u})-8c\int|x|^{-2}x\cdot\mathrm{Re}(u
abla ar{u}) -8\int x\cdot|u|^{p-1}\mathrm{Re}(u
abla ar{u}) \ &\equiv A+B+C. \end{split} \]
nodes.statement_short: Split the other term into $A+B+C$.

nodes.name: term $A$
nodes.statement:
Since $\partial_{x_k}(|\partial_{x_j}u|^2) = 2\mathrm{Re}(\partial_{x_j}u\partial_{x_j}\partial_{x_k} ar u)$ for $1\leqslant j,k\leqslant N$, we find  egin{align} A &= -8\sum_{j,k} \mathrm{Re}\int \partial_{x_j}^2u\, x_k\partial_{x_k} ar u = 8\sum_{j,k} \mathrm{Re}\int \partial_{x_j}u (\delta_{j,k}\partial_{x_k} ar u + x_k\partial_{x_j}\partial_{x_k} ar u) 
otag \ &= 8\sum_j \int |\partial_{x_j}u|^2 +4\sum_{j,k} \int x_k\partial_{x_k}(|\partial_{x_j}u|^2) 
otag \ &= 8\sum_j \int |\partial_{x_j}u|^2 -4\sum_{j,k} \int |\partial_{x_j}u|^2 = (8-4N)\int |
abla u|^2, \end{align} where $\delta_{j,k}=1$ for $j=k$ and $0$ otherwise.
nodes.statement_short: Compute $A=(8-4N)\int|\nabla u|^2$.

nodes.name: terms $C$ and $B$
nodes.statement_short: Compute $C$ and $B$ by integration by parts.

nodes.name: assemble
nodes.statement: Finally, putting together (\ref{viriala}), (\ref{virialpart3}), (\ref{virialc}) and (\ref{viriald}), we obtain \[ \begin{split} \Gamma''(t)&=8\int|\nabla u|^2-8c\int\frac{|u|^2}{|x|^2}+\frac{4}{p+1}(N-Np)\int|u|^{p+1} \\ &=16E(u)+\frac{4}{p+1}(N-Np+4)\int|u|^{p+1}, \end{split} \] which concludes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Sum the terms to get (4.16).

nodes.name: setup
nodes.statement: Let $u$ be a solution of \eqref{inls} such that $\|u\|_{L^2}=M_\mathrm{gs}$ and $\lim_{t\uparrow T} H(u) =+\infty$.
nodes.statement_short: Fix a minimal-mass solution blowing up at $T$.

nodes.name: Step 1: rescaled sequence converges
nodes.statement: {\em Step~1.} Let $\{t_n\}_{n\in\mathbb{N}} \subset \mathbb{R}$ be a sequence of times such that $t_n\uparrow T$ as $n\rightarrow\infty$. We set \[ u_n=u(t_n), \quad \lambda_n^2=H(u_n), \quad v_n(x)=\lambda_n^{-N/2}u_n(\lambda_n^{-1}x). \] We note that $\lambda_n\rightarrow\infty$ as $n\rightarrow\infty$, and $\|v_n\|_{L^2}=\|u_n\|_{L^2}=\|u_0\|_{L^2}=M_\mathrm{gs}$ by the $L^2$ scaling. Furthermore, \[ \begin{split} H(v_n)=\lambda_n^{-2}H(u_n)=1. \end{split} \] On the other hand, by conservation of the energy, \[ \begin{split} E(v_n)&=\frac12\lambda_n^{-2}H(u_n)-\frac{1}{p+1}\lambda_n^{-2}\int_{\mathbb{R}^N} |u_n(y)|^{p+1}dy\\ &=\lambda_n^{-2} E(u_n)=\lambda_n^{-2}E(u_0)\to 0 \quad \text{as} \ n\to\infty. \end{split} \] Hence, by Proposition \ref{compact.prop}, there exist $Q\in\mathcal{G}$, $\gamma_0\in\mathbb{R}$ and $\lambda_0>0$ such that, up to a subsequence, \begin{equation} \lim_{n\rightarrow\infty} \|v_n-e^{i\gamma_0}Q_{\lambda_0}\|_{H^1}=0, \end{equation} where $Q_{\lambda_0}(x)=\lambda_0^{N/2}Q(\lambda_0 x)$.
nodes.statement_short: Rescaled solutions along $t_n\to T$ converge to a ground state by Proposition 4.

nodes.name: rescaling
nodes.statement: {\em Step~1.} Let $\{t_n\}_{n\in\mathbb{N}} \subset \mathbb{R}$ be a sequence of times such that $t_n\uparrow T$ as $n\rightarrow\infty$. We set \[ u_n=u(t_n), \quad \lambda_n^2=H(u_n), \quad v_n(x)=\lambda_n^{-N/2}u_n(\lambda_n^{-1}x). \]
nodes.statement_short: Define $u_n$, $\lambda_n$, $v_n$.

nodes.name: properties of $v_n$
nodes.statement: We note that $\lambda_n\rightarrow\infty$ as $n\rightarrow\infty$, and $\|v_n\|_{L^2}=\|u_n\|_{L^2}=\|u_0\|_{L^2}=M_\mathrm{gs}$ by the $L^2$ scaling. Furthermore, \[ \begin{split} H(v_n)=\lambda_n^{-2}H(u_n)=1. \end{split} \] On the other hand, by conservation of the energy, \[ \begin{split} E(v_n)&=\frac12\lambda_n^{-2}H(u_n)-\frac{1}{p+1}\lambda_n^{-2}\int_{\mathbb{R}^N} |u_n(y)|^{p+1}dy\\ &=\lambda_n^{-2} E(u_n)=\lambda_n^{-2}E(u_0)\to 0 \quad \text{as} \ n\to\infty. \end{split} \]
nodes.statement_short: $v_n$ has minimal mass, $H(v_n)=1$, $E(v_n)\to0$.

nodes.name: apply compactness
nodes.statement: Hence, by Proposition \ref{compact.prop}, there exist $Q\in\mathcal{G}$, $\gamma_0\in\mathbb{R}$ and $\lambda_0>0$ such that, up to a subsequence, \begin{equation} \lim_{n\rightarrow\infty} \|v_n-e^{i\gamma_0}Q_{\lambda_0}\|_{H^1}=0, \end{equation} where $Q_{\lambda_0}(x)=\lambda_0^{N/2}Q(\lambda_0 x)$.
nodes.statement_short: Proposition 4 gives (4.23).

nodes.name: Step 2: mass concentration
nodes.statement: {\em Step~2.} We now prove that $u_n$ concentrates all of its mass at $x=0$ as $n\rightarrow\infty$. We show that, in the sense of distributions, \[ |u_n|^2\rightarrow M_\mathrm{gs}^2\delta_0. \] Indeed, for any $\varphi\in C^\infty_0(\mathbb{R}^N)$, using the change of variables $y=\lambda_n^{-1}x$ we find that \[ \begin{split} \int_{\mathbb{R}^N}|u_n(y)|^2\varphi(y)dy &=\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}|u_n(\lambda_n^{-1}x)|^2\varphi(\lambda^{-1}_nx)\lambda_n^{-N}dx =\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}|v_n(x)|^2\varphi(\lambda_n^{-1}x)dx\\ &=\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}(|v_n(x)|^2-|Q(x)|^2)\varphi(\lambda_n^{-1}x)dx+\int_{\mathbb{R}^N} |Q(x)|^2\varphi(0)dx\\ &\phantom{\leqslant} \ +\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}|Q(x)|^2(\varphi(\lambda_n^{-1}x)-\varphi(0))dx. \end{split} \] Thus, we obtain \[ \begin{split} \Big|\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}|u_n(y)|^2\varphi(y)dy -M_\mathrm{gs}^2\varphi(0)\Big| &\leqslant \|\varphi\|_{L^\infty}\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}||v_n(x)|^2-|Q(x)|^2|dx\\ &\phantom{\leqslant} \ +\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}|Q(x)|^2|\varphi(\lambda_n^{-1}x)-\varphi(0)|dx. \end{split} \] We conclude this step by noticing that $|v_n|^2$ converges strongly to $|Q|^2$ in $L^1(\mathbb{R}^N)$ from (\ref{b}), so the first integral vanishes as $n\rightarrow\infty$. Since $\lambda_n\rightarrow\infty$ the second integral also converges to zero by the dominated convergence theorem. Hence, we obtain \begin{equation} \int_{\mathbb{R}^N}|u_n(y)|^2\varphi(y)dy\rightarrow M_\mathrm{gs}^2\varphi(0). \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: $|u_n|^2\to M_{gs}^2\delta_0$ in distributions.

nodes.name: claim of concentration
nodes.statement: {\em Step~2.} We now prove that $u_n$ concentrates all of its mass at $x=0$ as $n\rightarrow\infty$. We show that, in the sense of distributions, \[ |u_n|^2\rightarrow M_\mathrm{gs}^2\delta_0. \]
nodes.statement_short: State the concentration claim.

nodes.name: change of variables
nodes.statement: Indeed, for any $\varphi\in C^\infty_0(\mathbb{R}^N)$, using the change of variables $y=\lambda_n^{-1}x$ we find that \[ \begin{split} \int_{\mathbb{R}^N}|u_n(y)|^2\varphi(y)dy &=\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}|u_n(\lambda_n^{-1}x)|^2\varphi(\lambda^{-1}_nx)\lambda_n^{-N}dx =\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}|v_n(x)|^2\varphi(\lambda_n^{-1}x)dx\\ &=\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}(|v_n(x)|^2-|Q(x)|^2)\varphi(\lambda_n^{-1}x)dx+\int_{\mathbb{R}^N} |Q(x)|^2\varphi(0)dx\\ &\phantom{\leqslant} \ +\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}|Q(x)|^2(\varphi(\lambda_n^{-1}x)-\varphi(0))dx. \end{split} \] Thus, we obtain \[ \begin{split} \Big|\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}|u_n(y)|^2\varphi(y)dy -M_\mathrm{gs}^2\varphi(0)\Big| &\leqslant \|\varphi\|_{L^\infty}\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}||v_n(x)|^2-|Q(x)|^2|dx\\ &\phantom{\leqslant} \ +\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}|Q(x)|^2|\varphi(\lambda_n^{-1}x)-\varphi(0)|dx. \end{split} \]
nodes.statement_short: Rewrite the pairing via $v_n$ and $Q$.

nodes.name: limits vanish
nodes.statement: We conclude this step by noticing that $|v_n|^2$ converges strongly to $|Q|^2$ in $L^1(\mathbb{R}^N)$ from (\ref{b}), so the first integral vanishes as $n\rightarrow\infty$. Since $\lambda_n\rightarrow\infty$ the second integral also converges to zero by the dominated convergence theorem. Hence, we obtain \begin{equation} \int_{\mathbb{R}^N}|u_n(y)|^2\varphi(y)dy\rightarrow M_\mathrm{gs}^2\varphi(0). \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Both error integrals vanish, giving (4.24).

nodes.name: Step 3: $u(t)\in\Sigma$ and variance formula
nodes.statement:
{\em Step~3.} We now show that $u(t)\in\Sigma$ for all $t\in[0,T)$. Let $\phi\in C^\infty_0(\mathbb{R}^N)$ be a radial and non-negative function such that $\phi(x)=|x|^2$ for $|x|\leqslant 1$. It is easy to see that there exists a constant $C>0$ such that \[ |
abla \phi (x) |^2\leqslant C\phi(x) \] for all $x\in\mathbb{R}^N$. Indeed, since $\phi$ is radially symmetric we may choose $f\in C(\mathbb{R},\mathbb{R}_+) $, such that $\phi(|x|)=f(|x|)$. By Taylor's formula, for all $r\in\mathbb{R}$ and $h\in\mathbb{R}$ there exists $y\in[r,r+h]$, such that \[ 0\leqslant f(r+h)=f(r)+f'(r)h+ rac{f''(y)}{2}h^2\leqslant f(r)+f'(r)h+C'h^2, \] where $C'=1+\max_{r\in\mathbb{R}} rac{|f'(r)|}{2}>0$. Since the right-hand side is a positive quadratic polynomial, we must have that $|f'(r)|^2-4C'f(r)\leqslant 0$, thus $|f'(r)|^2\leqslant Cf(r)$, where $C=4C'>0$. For all $R>0$, we define $\phi_R(x)=R^2\phi(x/R)$, and for all $t\in[0,T)$, \[ \Gamma_R(t)=\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}\phi_R(x)|u(t,x)|^2dx. \] A direct calculation, similar to the proof of Lemma~ef{virial.lemma}, yields that \[ \Gamma_R'(t)=2	ext{Re}\int\phi_R ar{u}\partial_tu =-2	ext{Im}\int\phi_R ar{u}(\Delta u+ rac{c}{|x|^2}u+|u|^{p-1}u) =2\int
abla\phi_R\cdot	ext{Im}( ar{u}
abla u). \] Since $\|u\|_{L^2}=\|Q\|_{L^2}$, we can apply Lemma ef{banica.lem} and the inequality $|
abla\phi_R|^2\leqslant C\phi_R$, to get \[ |\Gamma'_R(t)|\leqslant 2\sqrt{2E(u)}\Big(\int|
abla\phi_R|^2|u|^2\Big)^{1/2} \leqslant C\sqrt{E(u_0)}\sqrt{\Gamma_R(t)}. \] By integrating between a fixed $t\in[0,T)$ and $t_n$, we obtain, \[ |\sqrt{\Gamma_R(t)}-\sqrt{\Gamma_R(t_n)}|\leqslant C|t-t_n|. \] Applying (ef{c}) in Step 2, we get \[ \Gamma_R(t_n)=\int_{\mathbb{R}^N} |u_n(x)|^2\phi_R(x)dxightarrow M_\mathrm{gs}^2\phi_R(0)=0. \] Thus, letting $n	o\infty$ in the last inequality, we obtain, for all $t\in [0,T)$ and all $R>0$, \[ \Gamma_R(t) \leqslant C(T-t)^2. \] Since the right-hand side of the last expression is independent of $R$, letting $R	o\infty$ yields, for all $t\in [0,T)$, \[ u(t)\in\Sigma \quad	ext{and}\quad 0\leqslant \Gamma(t) \leqslant C(T-t)^2. \] From this estimate, we can extend by continuity $\Gamma(t)$ at $t=T$ by setting $\Gamma(T)=0$, from which we also obtain $\Gamma'(T)=0$. Moreover, since $u(t)\in\Sigma$ and $u$ is a solution of~\eqref{inls}, we may apply Lemma~ef{virial.lemma}, and by (ef{virialthree}) we obtain $\Gamma''(t)=16E(u_0)$, which finally gives, for all $t\in [0,T)$, \[ \Gamma(t) = 8E(u_0)(T-t)^2. \] Letting $t=0$, we find, using identity (ef{virialone}) \[ \Gamma(0)=\int |x|^2|u_0|^2= 8E(u_0)T^2 \quad 	ext{and}\quad \Gamma'(0)= 4\int x\cdot\mathrm{Im}(\overline{u_0}
abla u_0) = -16E(u_0)T. \]
nodes.statement_short: Localized virial plus Banica's lemma give $u(t)\in\Sigma$ and $\Gamma(t)=8E(u_0)(T-t)^2$.

nodes.name: cut-off function
nodes.statement: {\em Step~3.} We now show that $u(t)\in\Sigma$ for all $t\in[0,T)$. Let $\phi\in C^\infty_0(\mathbb{R}^N)$ be a radial and non-negative function such that $\phi(x)=|x|^2$ for $|x|\leqslant 1$.
nodes.statement_short: Claim $u(t)\in\Sigma$; choose a cut-off $\phi$.

nodes.name: gradient bound for $\phi$
nodes.statement: It is easy to see that there exists a constant $C>0$ such that \[ |\nabla \phi (x) |^2\leqslant C\phi(x) \] for all $x\in\mathbb{R}^N$. Indeed, since $\phi$ is radially symmetric we may choose $f\in C(\mathbb{R},\mathbb{R}_+) $, such that $\phi(|x|)=f(|x|)$. By Taylor's formula, for all $r\in\mathbb{R}$ and $h\in\mathbb{R}$ there exists $y\in[r,r+h]$, such that \[ 0\leqslant f(r+h)=f(r)+f'(r)h+\frac{f''(y)}{2}h^2\leqslant f(r)+f'(r)h+C'h^2, \] where $C'=1+\max_{r\in\mathbb{R}}\frac{|f'(r)|}{2}>0$. Since the right-hand side is a positive quadratic polynomial, we must have that $|f'(r)|^2-4C'f(r)\leqslant 0$, thus $|f'(r)|^2\leqslant Cf(r)$, where $C=4C'>0$.
nodes.statement_short: Taylor's formula gives $|\nabla\phi|^2\le C\phi$.

nodes.name: localized variance
nodes.statement: For all $R>0$, we define $\phi_R(x)=R^2\phi(x/R)$, and for all $t\in[0,T)$, \[ \Gamma_R(t)=\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}\phi_R(x)|u(t,x)|^2dx. \] A direct calculation, similar to the proof of Lemma~\ref{virial.lemma}, yields that \[ \Gamma_R'(t)=2\text{Re}\int\phi_R\bar{u}\partial_tu =-2\text{Im}\int\phi_R\bar{u}(\Delta u+\frac{c}{|x|^2}u+|u|^{p-1}u) =2\int\nabla\phi_R\cdot\text{Im}(\bar{u}\nabla u). \]
nodes.statement_short: Define $\Gamma_R$ and compute its derivative.

nodes.name: apply Banica's lemma
nodes.statement: Since $\|u\|_{L^2}=\|Q\|_{L^2}$, we can apply Lemma \ref{banica.lem} and the inequality $|\nabla\phi_R|^2\leqslant C\phi_R$, to get \[ |\Gamma'_R(t)|\leqslant 2\sqrt{2E(u)}\Big(\int|\nabla\phi_R|^2|u|^2\Big)^{1/2} \leqslant C\sqrt{E(u_0)}\sqrt{\Gamma_R(t)}. \] By integrating between a fixed $t\in[0,T)$ and $t_n$, we obtain, \[ |\sqrt{\Gamma_R(t)}-\sqrt{\Gamma_R(t_n)}|\leqslant C|t-t_n|. \]
nodes.statement_short: Banica's lemma bounds $|\Gamma_R'|$ by $C\sqrt{\Gamma_R}$; integrate.

nodes.name: uniform bound on $\Gamma_R$
nodes.statement: Applying (\ref{c}) in Step 2, we get \[ \Gamma_R(t_n)=\int_{\mathbb{R}^N} |u_n(x)|^2\phi_R(x)dx\rightarrow M_\mathrm{gs}^2\phi_R(0)=0. \] Thus, letting $n\to\infty$ in the last inequality, we obtain, for all $t\in [0,T)$ and all $R>0$, \[ \Gamma_R(t) \leqslant C(T-t)^2. \] Since the right-hand side of the last expression is independent of $R$, letting $R\to\infty$ yields, for all $t\in [0,T)$, \[ u(t)\in\Sigma \quad\text{and}\quad 0\leqslant \Gamma(t) \leqslant C(T-t)^2. \]
nodes.statement_short: Mass concentration gives $\Gamma_R(t)\le C(T-t)^2$, so $u(t)\in\Sigma$.

nodes.name: virial identity
nodes.statement: From this estimate, we can extend by continuity $\Gamma(t)$ at $t=T$ by setting $\Gamma(T)=0$, from which we also obtain $\Gamma'(T)=0$. Moreover, since $u(t)\in\Sigma$ and $u$ is a solution of~\eqref{inls}, we may apply Lemma~\ref{virial.lemma}, and by (\ref{virialthree}) we obtain $\Gamma''(t)=16E(u_0)$, which finally gives, for all $t\in [0,T)$, \[ \Gamma(t) = 8E(u_0)(T-t)^2. \] Letting $t=0$, we find, using identity (\ref{virialone}) \[ \Gamma(0)=\int |x|^2|u_0|^2= 8E(u_0)T^2 \quad \text{and}\quad \Gamma'(0)= 4\int x\cdot\mathrm{Im}(\overline{u_0}\nabla u_0) = -16E(u_0)T. \]
nodes.statement_short: Virial identities give $\Gamma(t)=8E(u_0)(T-t)^2$ and values at $t=0$.

nodes.name: Step 4: identification via pseudo-conformal transformation
nodes.statement: {\em Step 4.} We apply identity \eqref{valeria} with $u_0$, $s=\frac{1}{2T}$, and $\theta(x)=\frac{|x|^2}{2}$ to get \[ \begin{split} E(u_0e^{i\frac{|x|^2}{4T}})&=E(u_0)+\frac{1}{2T}\int x\cdot\text{Im}(\bar{u_0}\nabla u_0) +\frac{1}{8T^2}\int|x|^2|u_0|^2\\ &=E(u_0)+\frac{1}{2T}(-4E(u_0))+\frac{1}{8T^2}(8E(u_0)T^2)=0. \end{split} \] Note that this calculation justifies, {\em a posteriori}, the application of~\eqref{valeria} with $\theta(x)=\frac{|x|^2}{2}\not\in C_0^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^N)$. Since $\|u_0e^{i\frac{|x|^2}{4T}}\|_{L^2}=M_\mathrm{gs}$ and $E(u_0e^{i\frac{|x|^2}{4T}})=0$, we can deduce from Proposition \ref{charact.prop} that there exist $\lambda_1>0$, $\gamma_1\in\mathbb{R}$, and $\widetilde{Q}\in\mathcal{G}$ such that \[ u_0(x)=e^{i\gamma_1}e^{-i\frac{|x|^2}{4T}}\lambda_1^{N/2}\widetilde{Q}(\lambda_1x). \] Finally, we use the pseudo-conformal transformation. We define $\tilde\lambda_0=\lambda_1T>0$ and $\tilde\gamma_0=\gamma_1-\lambda_1^2T\in\mathbb{R}$, and write $u_0$ as \[ u_0(x)=e^{i\tilde\gamma_0}e^{i\frac{\tilde\lambda^2_0}{T}} e^{-i\frac{|x|^2}{4T}}\Big(\frac{\tilde\lambda_0}{T}\Big)^{N/2}\widetilde{Q}\Big(\frac{\tilde\lambda_0x}{T}\Big). \] Thus, $u_0=S_{\widetilde{Q},T,\tilde\lambda_0,\tilde\gamma_0}(0)$, where $S_{\widetilde{Q},T,\tilde\lambda_0,\tilde\gamma_0}$ is defined by (\ref{S2.def}). By invoking uniqueness of the solution of (\ref{inls}), we find that $u(t)=S_{\widetilde{Q},T,\tilde\lambda_0,\tilde\gamma_0}(t)$ for all $t\in[0,T)$, which concludes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: $u_0e^{i|x|^2/4T}$ has zero energy, so is a ground state; uniqueness gives $u=S$.

nodes.name: zero energy of the modulated datum
nodes.statement: {\em Step 4.} We apply identity \eqref{valeria} with $u_0$, $s=\frac{1}{2T}$, and $\theta(x)=\frac{|x|^2}{2}$ to get \[ \begin{split} E(u_0e^{i\frac{|x|^2}{4T}})&=E(u_0)+\frac{1}{2T}\int x\cdot\text{Im}(\bar{u_0}\nabla u_0) +\frac{1}{8T^2}\int|x|^2|u_0|^2\\ &=E(u_0)+\frac{1}{2T}(-4E(u_0))+\frac{1}{8T^2}(8E(u_0)T^2)=0. \end{split} \] Note that this calculation justifies, {\em a posteriori}, the application of~\eqref{valeria} with $\theta(x)=\frac{|x|^2}{2}\not\in C_0^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^N)$.
nodes.statement_short: Apply (4.22) to get $E(u_0e^{i|x|^2/4T})=0$.

nodes.name: variational characterization
nodes.statement: Since $\|u_0e^{i\frac{|x|^2}{4T}}\|_{L^2}=M_\mathrm{gs}$ and $E(u_0e^{i\frac{|x|^2}{4T}})=0$, we can deduce from Proposition \ref{charact.prop} that there exist $\lambda_1>0$, $\gamma_1\in\mathbb{R}$, and $\widetilde{Q}\in\mathcal{G}$ such that \[ u_0(x)=e^{i\gamma_1}e^{-i\frac{|x|^2}{4T}}\lambda_1^{N/2}\widetilde{Q}(\lambda_1x). \]
nodes.statement_short: Proposition 3 identifies $u_0$.

nodes.name: pseudo-conformal form
nodes.statement: Finally, we use the pseudo-conformal transformation. We define $\tilde\lambda_0=\lambda_1T>0$ and $\tilde\gamma_0=\gamma_1-\lambda_1^2T\in\mathbb{R}$, and write $u_0$ as \[ u_0(x)=e^{i\tilde\gamma_0}e^{i\frac{\tilde\lambda^2_0}{T}} e^{-i\frac{|x|^2}{4T}}\Big(\frac{\tilde\lambda_0}{T}\Big)^{N/2}\widetilde{Q}\Big(\frac{\tilde\lambda_0x}{T}\Big). \] Thus, $u_0=S_{\widetilde{Q},T,\tilde\lambda_0,\tilde\gamma_0}(0)$, where $S_{\widetilde{Q},T,\tilde\lambda_0,\tilde\gamma_0}$ is defined by (\ref{S2.def}).
nodes.statement_short: Rewrite $u_0=S(0)$.

nodes.name: uniqueness
nodes.statement: By invoking uniqueness of the solution of (\ref{inls}), we find that $u(t)=S_{\widetilde{Q},T,\tilde\lambda_0,\tilde\gamma_0}(t)$ for all $t\in[0,T)$, which concludes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Uniqueness gives $u=S$.
